newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF confirms securitised land report.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF confirms securitised land report.

text.p: A senior Finance Ministry official confirmed on Monday a report that the government plans to permit the securitisation of collateralised land used for commercial purposes to boost liquidity in the property market.

The Nihon Keizai Shimbun financial daily reported on Monday the measure, which would take effect in April, would form the main part of the package that the government said would be announced at the end of March.
The official told Reuters that the ministry also plans to allow for the establishment of special purpose companies to take over foreclosed property, and to issue bonds.

The ministry is considering exempting special purpose companies from corporate taxes and taxes on the acquisition of property, but a final decision on the taxes will be made when the overall tax system is reviewed later this year for the 1998/99 fiscal year, he said.

The official said: "There is a widespread view among overseas investors that Japan's land prices have bottomed out. Deregulation and more disclosure will make if possible to issue securities at low cost, making them attractive to foreign investors."

Credits backed by collateralised land will be securitised through trust banks and the securities can be sold to investors in small lots. The property-backed securities will also be sold to investors by brokers and banks, he said.
"Details will be discussed with the Tokyo Stock Exchange, but those securities may be able to be listed on the exchange as corporate bonds," the official said.
He also said that the bonds, authorised as securities under the law, will also be a component of investment trust funds, which are likely to attract individual investors.
Bond transactions securitised through trust banks will be tax-exempt from April, he added.
The official said that Nikko Securities Co Ltd was working to securitise collateralised property-backed credits from May.
A Nikko spokesman declined to comment.

The official said that while problem loans held by the Housing Loan Administration Corp and the Resolution and Collection Bank are promising candidates for the securitisation programme, collateralised property owned by regional and second-tier regional banks might be securitised first.
